verdicts.why: The claim's core assertion ('exhausting heap memory regardless of frame size declaration') is false: line 147 wraps the stream in TruncatedInputStream(in, tableLength) so the loop can consume at most tableLength bytes (and only as many as the peer actually delivers), and every entry costs >= 2 wire bytes; worse for the attacker, the containsKey dedup at line 151 means only DISTINCT names become entries, so 1,000,000 keys requires names >= 3 bytes, i.e. >= 5MB of real wire data. Growth is proportional to bytes received, not unbounded.

The overflow is real Java semantics but grants the attacker nothing: the peer already chooses the entire 64-bit value at line 269, and non-overflowing inputs already span the full java.util.Date range (+/-2^63 ms), so 'accepting stale/future-dated messages' is reachable without any wrap. No memory, control-flow, or capability delta.

The 'infinite loop' half is refuted in-file (readFieldValue consumes >= 1 byte per iteration from a stream bounded by line 242, and exhaustion throws EOFException at line 161), but whether available() under-reports and truncates the array depends on TruncatedInputStream.available() and the underlying stream, neither of which is present in the target (only ValueReader.java and pom.xml exist).

Line 151 implements a deliberate, deterministic first-wins policy and the claim describes it correctly; what it asks for is a log line or counter, with no attacker capability and no stated concrete impact ('can hide ... attacks' is speculation). That is a diagnostics preference, not a defect.

Factually wrong: InputStream.read() returns 0..255 for a data byte (0xFF -> 255, positive) and -1 only at EOF, so the two ARE distinguishable, and the guard at line 231 ((ch1|ch2|ch3|ch4) < 0 over longs) catches any -1 before the arithmetic; the claim itself concedes 'the logic is correct'.

I could not refute it: line 88 allocates new byte[(int)contentLength] BEFORE readFully at line 89, so a wrapping TruncatedInputStream does not prevent the allocation, and the only check (line 87, contentLength < Integer.MAX_VALUE) still admits ~2GB from a 4-byte attacker-controlled length prefix.

The claim's premise is impossible: scale comes from in.readUnsignedByte() at line 172, so it is bounded to 0..255 and can never be 'greater than Integer.MAX_VALUE' or negative, and the unscaled magnitude is fixed at exactly 4 bytes by line 173, so there is no unbounded BigInteger/BigDecimal.

At the cited location (line 68) the length is in.readUnsignedByte(), bounded to 0..255 - the claim's own evidence concedes this is 'acceptable'; the line-88 concern it pivots to is a different call site and is filed separately as C06.

Same refutation as C02 and there is no HIGH-severity mechanism: the wrap at line 269 produces a Date the peer could already produce directly (readLong is fully attacker-chosen and Date covers +/-292M years), and no memory, parsing, or control-flow consequence follows; 'timing-based attacks' names no attack.

The stated mechanism is false: if 1-3 bytes are read before EOF, the EOF read returns -1, whose long value has every bit set, so (ch1|ch2|ch3|ch4) is negative and line 231 throws EOFException before any bitwise construction; the 'race condition in multi-threaded environments' is not created by this method (DataInputStream.readInt() has identical semantics) and readInt() is not a substitute since this must return an unsigned 32-bit value as a long.

Factually backwards about the code: line 151-152 is 'if(!table.containsKey(name)) table.put(name, value)', which KEEPS the first value and drops later duplicates; earlier values are never overwritten and 'early values are lost' is the opposite of what executes.

The attack requires a large negative scale, which line 172's in.readUnsignedByte() makes impossible (0..255, never negative - as the claim itself concedes mid-evidence); moreover BigDecimal(BigInteger,int) merely stores the int scale and allocates nothing proportional to it.

No defect: UTF-8 is mandatory in every Java platform implementation, and UnsupportedEncodingException extends IOException so it is already covered by the method's 'throws IOException' at line 66 and propagates correctly; the rest is a defensiveness/style preference with no attacker.

The claim states outright that 'the logic is correct' and objects only to readability/audit surface, and its equivalence premise is wrong: readInt() returns a signed int while readUnsignedInt must return 0..2^32-1 as a long (line 233). Style preference, no impact.

I could not find any depth counter or guard: case 'F' (line 181) -> readTable (139) -> readFieldValue (150) and case 'A' (line 184) -> readArray (237) -> readFieldValue (245) recurse with only ~5-6 wire bytes per nesting level, and nothing in the file bounds the depth.

Same as C02/C09: line 269's wrap changes nothing an attacker could not already achieve by sending a different readLong value, and no legitimate peer can emit seconds > 9.2e15 (year ~292,000,000), so there is neither an attack nor a benign trigger.

A scale of Integer.MAX_VALUE is unreachable: line 172 reads it with in.readUnsignedByte(), bounding it to 0..255, and with the unscaled value fixed at 4 bytes (line 173) even scale=255 is a harmless BigDecimal with no performance or precision consequence.

The description of lines 148 and 244 is accurate, but whether available() ever under-reports and truncates parsing is a property of TruncatedInputStream.available() and of the stream that ValueReader is constructed over (line 57), and neither source is in the target - it contains only ValueReader.java and pom.xml.

The stated trigger is factually wrong: DataInputStream.readFully throws EOFException when the stream is exhausted (lines 69, 89, 174), it does not hang; a stall without EOF is a socket-level SO_TIMEOUT concern that a parser reading a generic DataInputStream (line 57) cannot and should not enforce.

'Grow unbounded' is false and the claim's own numbers show it: the loop reads through TruncatedInputStream(in, tableLength) (lines 146-147) so it consumes at most tableLength bytes at >= 2 bytes per entry, and the dedup at line 151 caps the map at the number of distinct names - heap use is proportional (~10x) to bytes the peer actually sent, not unbounded.

Same as C18: the code does use available() at lines 148 and 244 as described, but deciding whether TruncatedInputStream.available() can return 0 with bytes remaining requires that class and the concrete underlying stream, neither of which exists in the target directory.

Pure style/micro-performance preference with no attacker and no impact; the charset name at line 70 is resolved by a cached lookup and a misspelling would surface as an IOException already declared at line 66 - StandardCharsets is a readability nicety, not a defect.

I tried to find a bound and there is none: nothing between readFieldValue (line 158), readTable (139) and readArray (237) tracks depth, and each nesting level of 'A' costs only 5 wire bytes (type octet + 4-byte length), so a modest payload yields thousands of stack frames.

Not a defect - it is required behaviour: the TruncatedInputStream at lines 146-147 and 241-242 owns no resource of its own, it merely filters the caller's already-open stream, so closing it would close the shared connection stream mid-parse; the wrapper is plain heap garbage.

Could not be refuted: readFieldValue's case 'F' (line 181) and case 'A' (line 184) re-enter readFieldValue through readTable/readArray with no depth counter anywhere in the file, and the per-level wire cost is ~5-6 bytes, so bounded input produces unbounded recursion depth.

'Unbounded' is false: lines 241-242 bound the loop to `length` bytes actually delivered and every element costs >= 1 wire byte (the cheapest being 'V'), so the ArrayList grows in fixed proportion (~4-8x) to bytes the peer sent - the claim's own 10MB example yields tens of MB, i.e. self-limiting, not exhaustion.

The premise is inverted: line 87 uses strict '<', so contentLength == Integer.MAX_VALUE falls to the else branch and throws UnsupportedOperationException (line 92) - it never reaches line 88; and for every admitted value the (int) cast is exact and non-negative, so no NegativeArraySizeException path exists, as the claim's own evidence admits.

The 'infinite loop' half is impossible in-file (each iteration consumes >= 1 byte via readUnsignedByte at line 161 from a stream capped at tableLength, and exhaustion raises EOFException), but the premature-truncation half turns entirely on TruncatedInputStream.available(), a class referenced at line 147 and absent from the target.
